newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: NEWCREST LOOKING FOR CHIEF, FUNDING BY OCT.
newsitem.headline: NEWCREST LOOKING FOR CHIEF, FUNDING BY OCT.

text.p: Newcrest Mining Ltd said on Tuesday it was looking to have secured A$600 million in funding for several major projects and a permanent new chief executive by its annual meeting, due in mid-October.

"That is the deadline we have set ourselves and we hope to achieve it, easily if we can, on both those major issues," chief executive Ian Johnson told Reuters from Melbourne. He said negotiations were at an advanced stage on both matters.

Johnson said the company was continuing negotiations with its bankers to secure A$600 million in funding to develop the A$440 million Cadia Hill/Ridgeway project in New South Wales, the A$90 million Gosowong project in Indonesia, and its 22 percent stake in the Boddington mine in Western Australia.
"We have not received that funding as yet ... and how close we are, of course we do not know," he said.
"We are very hopeful we can get it," he said.
Johnson said that if necessary, Newcrest would consider seeking a partner in one or more developments, or selling assets.

"The first step in all that is to get the debt facility in place and then if the decision is made to seek a partner - and I stress that decision has not been made - we would clearly be in a much stronger position to negotiate," he said.
Johnson said Newcrest would prefer to maintain its stake in Boddington, but it was likely to be the first asset to be sold if development funds were needed for the other priorities.
While Newcrest's troubled Telfer mine in July had met budget both in expenditure and gold ounces produced, the Cadia and Gosowong projects were the company's future, he said.
"We like the project a great deal ... but if it means that Boddington takes funds we do not have for Cadia or Gosowong, Boddington would have to take a back seat for us," he said.

While fellow stakeholder Normandy Mining Ltd has been touted as a likely buyer to boost its current 44 percent holding, Johnson said Newcrest had received no recent offers for the stake since rejecting an earlier approach.

Johnson was appointed as caretaker chief executive in May, following the sudden resignation of predecessor John Quinn whose last months in office were dogged by criticism of Telfer's performance and a costly investment in Normandy.
